q: Which term describes the downward-acting vertical forces from gravity, comprising permanent dead loads (self-weight of slabs, frames, walls, and fixed equipment) plus temporary live loads (occupants, movable furniture, stored goods)?
n: Gravity loads are the dead and live loads acting downward; lateral loads act sideways.

q: Since a shear wall resists lateral force acting parallel to its own plane, where is it typically best positioned within a high-rise building?
n: Shear walls around elevator and stair shafts form a stiff central core that resists lateral load from every direction.

q: When a beam has so much tension steel that the concrete crushes before the steel yields, the failure is sudden. What is this condition called?
n: Over-reinforced beams fail by concrete crushing without warning, so codes limit steel to keep beams under-reinforced and ductile.

q: What classification applies to occupancies or structures that house toxic chemicals or explosive materials?
n: Hazardous facilities (Occupancy Category II) house toxic or explosive materials whose release would endanger the public.

q: Complete the statement: forces acting horizontally on a structure, produced by environmental effects such as wind and earthquakes, are known as ___.
n: Wind and earthquake push a building sideways, so their forces are lateral loads.

q: What term names a wall built specifically to hold back soil or other loose material from moving laterally?
n: A retaining wall holds back earth on one side, resisting its lateral pressure.

q: A roughly horizontal structural system that transfers lateral forces to the vertical elements resisting them, including horizontal bracing systems, is called a:
n: Floors and roofs act as diaphragms, collecting lateral forces and passing them to the walls and frames.

q: Fill in the blank: a story whose lateral stiffness is less than 70% of the stiffness of the story immediately above it is called a ___ story.
n: A soft story is less than 70% as stiff as the story above (or 80% of the average of the three above).

q: What is it called when a story's strength is less than 80% of the strength of the story above it?
n: A weak story has less than 80% of the strength of the story above.

q: What term describes the secondary effect on member shears, axial forces, and moments caused by vertical loads acting through the horizontal displacement of a structure?
n: Gravity load acting on a displaced frame adds extra moment: load P times sway Δ.

q: What do we call the artificial stone produced by properly proportioning hydraulic cement, fine and coarse aggregates, and water, with or without admixtures?
n: Concrete is the artificial stone of cement, aggregates and water.

q: A substance other than cement, water, or aggregate, added to concrete before or during mixing to modify its properties, is known as a/an:
n: An admixture is added before or during mixing to change setting, workability or other properties.

q: Building and fabricating with stone, clay, brick, or concrete block — also referring generally to construction with poured concrete — is called:
n: Masonry works are construction with stone, brick, clay tile or concrete block.

q: What is the name for a beam that carries the load of material above a door or window opening?
n: A lintel spans over a door or window and carries the wall above it.

q: What property lets a material be stretched a long way without breaking?
n: Ductility is large permanent stretch before fracture. Elasticity is springing back when the load is removed; malleability is being hammered into sheets.

q: What do you call the sudden sharp bending or buckling that occurs when a column is loaded excessively?
n: Crippling is the sudden local buckling or collapse of a slender compression member.

q: Which mode of failure is typical for a short concrete column?
n: Short columns fail by crushing the concrete; long columns fail by buckling.

q: Also called cold flow, this is the gradual, permanent deformation of a solid material under sustained stress below its yield strength, often linked to high temperature. What is it?
n: Creep is slow, permanent deformation under a sustained load.

q: What term refers to reinforcing bars placed in contact so they act as a single unit?
n: Up to four bars tied in contact act as one bundled bar.

q: What flat horizontal structural element, usually reinforced with steel mesh or rebar, is used for floors, ceilings, roofs, and building or pavement bases?
n: A slab is a flat horizontal element that carries loads by bending.

q: Besides resisting vertical and diagonal tension in a beam, what other function do stirrups serve?
n: Stirrups carry shear and also hold the longitudinal bars in position during casting.

q: Honeycombing in concrete can be reduced through what mechanical means of compaction?
n: Vibrators consolidate fresh concrete, driving out air pockets that cause honeycombing.

q: Where are earthquake effects usually most severe?
o: In deep ravines far from faults
Near large bodies of water only
n: Ground rupture and the strongest shaking occur near the fault that slipped.

q: Which structural element typically uses ties as lateral reinforcement?
n: Ties are the lateral reinforcement of tied columns; beams use stirrups.

q: What is a column that does not line up with the column below it, starting instead on a beam, called?
n: A planted (floating) column transfers its load into a beam, which must be designed for it. Planted columns are weak points in earthquakes.

q: Which prestressing method tensions the reinforcement before the concrete is cast?
n: In pre-tensioning, tendons are stretched before the concrete is cast and released once it hardens.

q: A frame system in which beams, slabs, columns, and joints resist forces predominantly through shear, flexure, and axial force — with beams/slabs mostly horizontal and columns mostly vertical — is called a:
n: A moment frame resists loads through flexure, shear and axial force in rigidly joined beams and columns.

q: When a heavily loaded column punches a hole through its supporting base, what type of failure is this?
n: A heavily loaded column can punch through its footing or slab along a cone-shaped surface: punching (two-way) shear.

q: The shear stress at a reinforcing bar's surface that prevents relative slip between the bar and surrounding concrete — the adhesion force per unit contact area between the bonded surfaces — is called:
n: Bond stress is the shear stress between the bar surface and the surrounding concrete.

q: What is the name for reinforcement used in beams to resist shear and torsion — typically deformed bars or wire bent into L, U, or rectangular shapes and placed perpendicular or at an angle to the longitudinal bars (called a “tie” in tied columns)?
n: Stirrups resist shear and torsion in beams; the same bars in columns are called ties.

q: What do you call the temporary force applied by a device to introduce tension into prestressing tendons?
n: The jacking force is the temporary force applied by the jack to tension a tendon.

q: Concrete used for structural purposes, covering both plain and reinforced concrete, is termed:
n: Structural concrete covers all concrete used structurally, plain or reinforced.

q: In geotechnical engineering, the gradual vertical movement of the ground — usually from changes in stress, most likely when added vertical stress is applied over soft or loose soil — is known as:
n: Settlement is the downward movement of the ground as soil compresses under load.

q: What term describes soil's capacity to let water pass through it?
n: Permeability measures how easily water flows through soil.

q: Besides checking consistency, what property of fresh concrete does a slump test primarily assess?
n: The slump test measures the workability (consistency) of fresh concrete.

q: Which admixture delays the onset of hardening and slows the hydration rate of concrete?
n: A retarder slows setting, useful in hot weather or long hauls.

q: Inert materials that make up about 60–75% of the volume of concrete are called:
n: Fine and coarse aggregate together fill most of the volume; cement paste binds them.

q: Which type of wall is designed to carry vertical loads?
n: A load-bearing wall carries vertical loads from floors and roofs above.

q: What is the name for a formed, sawed, or tooled groove in concrete meant to create a weakened plane and control where cracking occurs due to dimensional change?
n: A contraction (control) joint is a planned weak line where shrinkage cracks can form neatly.

q: What is the term for the length of embedded reinforcement required to develop the design strength of the bar at a critical section?
n: Development length is the embedment needed for bond to develop the bar's design stress.

q: Which prestressing method tensions the tendons only after the concrete has hardened?
n: In post-tensioning, tendons in ducts are stressed after the concrete has hardened.

q: What material encases prestressing reinforcement to keep it from bonding with the surrounding concrete, provide corrosion protection, and contain a corrosion-inhibiting coating?
n: Sheathing encloses unbonded tendons, keeps them from bonding and protects them from corrosion.

q: Working stress is the actual stress a material experiences under a given load. What term names the maximum stress the material can safely withstand?
n: Allowable stress is the safe limit: the material strength divided by a factor of safety.

q: The stress that results from a restrained deformation caused by a change in temperature is called:
n: Restraining thermal expansion or contraction creates thermal stress.

q: What is the name for reinforcement continuously wound in the shape of a cylindrical helix?
n: Spiral reinforcement is a continuous helix that confines a column core.

q: What is the term for a point in a beam or column where no moment develops — a point where the direction of curvature changes?
n: At an inflection point the moment is zero and the curvature changes direction.

q: What do you call a long wall or embankment built to prevent flooding from bodies of water?
n: A dike is an embankment built along water to prevent flooding.

q: A bracing configuration where a pair of braces above or below a beam meet at a single point within the beam's clear span is called:
n: Chevron (inverted-V or V) bracing has two braces meeting at one point along the beam span.

q: What is the term for an upright compression member whose unsupported height does not exceed 3 times its least lateral dimension?
n: A pedestal is a compression member no taller than 3 times its least lateral dimension.

q: A joint — often about ½ inch wide and filled with cork or recycled fiber — that separates a new concrete slab or wall from an existing one is called a/an:
n: An isolation joint separates new concrete from existing elements so each can move freely.

q: What connection method fuses steel members together and joins components of a built-up member (such as a plate girder) using heat in a controlled atmosphere, requiring skilled labor?
n: Welding fuses steel parts with heat and needs skilled, certified welders.

q: A knot found in wood or timber is classified as what type of defect?
n: Knots grow with the tree, so they are natural defects, not seasoning or handling defects.

q: For deformed bars from 10 mm through 25 mm Ø, the minimum bend diameter must equal:
n: Bars 10–25 mm need a 6db inside bend diameter; 28–36 mm need 8db; larger bars 10db.

q: What is the maximum allowable spacing of spirals?
n: Clear spacing between spiral turns must be 25 to 75 mm.

q: What is the strength reduction factor, Ø, used for flexure?
n: Tension-controlled sections, such as beams in flexure, use φ = 0.90.

q: What is the maximum spacing of main flexural bars in a one-way slab?
n: NSCP 2015 limits primary slab bars to 3 times the slab thickness or 450 mm, whichever is smaller. Shrinkage bars may go to 5h or 450 mm.

q: A slab is classified as one-way when the ratio of width to length, m, satisfies:
n: m = short span ÷ long span; below 0.5 the slab bends mainly one way.

q: A slab is classified as two-way when the ratio of width to length, m, satisfies:
n: When m is 0.5 or more, the slab bends significantly in both directions: two-way.

q: What is the minimum longitudinal reinforcement requirement for a tied column?
n: Tied columns need at least 4 bars (3 in triangular ties); 16 mm is a common minimum size.

q: What is the minimum longitudinal reinforcement requirement for a spirally reinforced column?
n: Spiral columns need at least 6 longitudinal bars.

q: Structural steel with a yield stress of 36,000 psi carries which ASTM designation?
n: ASTM A36 steel has a yield stress of 36 ksi (about 250 MPa).

q: What is the minimum thickness of a two-way slab without beams when drop panels are provided?
n: Without drop panels the minimum is 125 mm. Drop panels thicken the slab at the columns, so the rest may be thinner.

q: For slabs not exposed to weather and not in contact with the ground, what is the minimum clear concrete cover required?
n: Slabs not exposed to weather or ground need 20 mm of cover.

q: Under the NSCP, the nominal maximum size of coarse aggregate must not exceed the least of three limits. Which set is correct?
o: 1/5 the narrowest form dimension, 1/3 the slab depth, 3/4 the minimum clear bar spacing
1/3 the narrowest form dimension, 1/5 the slab depth, 1/2 the minimum clear bar spacing
1/4 the narrowest form dimension, 1/2 the slab depth, 2/3 the minimum clear bar spacing
n: Aggregate size is limited to 1/5 of the narrowest form dimension, 1/3 of slab depth and 3/4 of clear bar spacing.

q: A 28-day concrete strength of 3,000 psi is about how many MPa?
Grade 60 reinforcing steel has a yield stress of 414 MPa, which converts to:
n: Grade 60 means a yield stress of 60 ksi, about 414 MPa (Grade 420).

q: What is the strength reduction factor, Ø, applicable to shear and torsion?
n: Shear and torsion use φ = 0.75.

q: ASTM Type I cement is typically specified for:
n: Type I is ordinary portland cement for general use.

q: What is the diameter of a No. 8 deformed reinforcing bar?
n: Bar numbers are eighths of an inch: No. 8 is 1 in, about 25 mm.

q: Concrete cast directly against and permanently exposed to earth requires a minimum cover of:
n: Concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth needs 75 mm of cover.

q: What is the minimum length of any tension lap splice of deformed bars?
n: Class A splices are 1.0 ld and Class B are 1.3 ld, but never less than 300 mm.

q: Bundling is not permitted for deformed bars larger than ___ mm.
n: Bars larger than 36 mm may not be bundled in beams.

q: The minimum clear spacing between parallel bars in one layer is d<sub>b</sub>, but never less than:
n: Clear spacing between parallel bars in a layer is the larger of 25 mm, db and 4/3 of aggregate size.

q: What is the maximum number of bars allowed in a bundle?
n: A bundle may contain at most four bars.

q: For a simply supported beam of length L carrying a uniformly distributed load w (N/m), what is the maximum bending moment?
n: For a simply supported beam with uniform load, Mmax = wL²/8 at midspan.

q: The minimum length for a Class A tension lap splice is ___, but never less than 300 mm.
n: A Class A tension splice is 1.0 ld; Class B is 1.3 ld; both at least 300 mm.

q: What type of welding fuses metal studs or similar parts to steel using heat from an electric arc, with a ceramic ferrule at the stud's end containing shielding flux?
n: Stud welding fuses studs using an arc, with a ceramic ferrule holding flux at the stud end.

q: If a beam pour cannot be finished in one operation, where should the construction joint be placed?
o: At the face of the support
Within the middle third of the span
At the point of maximum shear
At the end of the cantilever
n: Shear is lowest in the middle third of the span, so a joint there is least likely to slip.

q: What do you call two or more materials combined together to act as one?
n: A composite member combines materials, such as steel and concrete, to act as one.

q: What loads must a curtain wall be designed to resist?
n: Curtain walls carry no floor loads, only their own weight and the wind (and seismic) forces on them.

q: What web reinforcement resists vertical and diagonal tension in a beam while holding the main bars in place?
n: Stirrups resist diagonal tension from shear and hold the main bars in place.

q: Which type of column is most prone to failure by buckling?
n: Long, slender columns fail by buckling before the material crushes.

q: What is the distance from the extreme compression fiber to the centroid of tension reinforcement called?
n: Effective depth d is measured from the compression face to the centroid of the tension steel.

q: A loop of reinforcing bar or wire that encloses the longitudinal bars in a tied column is known as a:
n: Ties are closed loops of bar that enclose the longitudinal bars of a tied column.

q: What vertical element encloses or separates spaces and can also serve as a structural member?
n: A wall encloses or divides space and may also carry loads.

q: The Occupancy Importance Factor, I<sub>p</sub>, is normally 1.0, except for Hazardous and Essential Facilities, where it equals:
n: Components in essential and hazardous facilities use Ip = 1.5; all others 1.0.

q: What inert material is mixed with hydraulic cement and water to produce concrete?
n: Aggregate is the inert filler mixed with cement and water to make concrete.

q: In a spirally reinforced column, the clear spacing (pitch) between spirals must not exceed 75mm and must not be less than:
n: Spiral clear spacing: at least 25 mm, at most 75 mm.

q: What method introduces a jacking force by tensioning tendons only after the concrete has hardened enough to sustain the load?
n: Post-tensioning stresses the tendons after the concrete can take the force.

q: What is the mass of a 1 m length of 12 mm deformed bar?
n: Bar mass per metre is d²/162 (kg/m, d in mm).

q: The intensity of force per unit area is termed:
n: Stress is force per unit area.

q: What term names the length of reinforcement, mechanical anchor, hook, or a combination thereof, extending beyond the point of zero stress in the bar?
n: End anchorage is the embedment, hook or device beyond the point of zero stress that anchors a bar.

q: A 3-second gust speed measured 10 meters above the ground in Exposure C, with a 0.02 annual probability of being exceeded (50-year mean recurrence interval), defines the:
n: Basic wind speed is a 3-second gust at 10 m in Exposure C with a 50-year return period.

q: What is the displacement of one level relative to the level above or below it called?
n: Story drift is the lateral displacement of one level relative to the next.

q: Splices of deformed bars must be staggered by at least ___, developing at every section at least twice the calculated tensile force but not less than 140 MPa for the total reinforcement area provided.
n: Staggered splices spread the weak points so no one section is spliced in full.

q: What is a continuous reinforcing bar with a seismic hook at one end and a hook of at least 90 degrees plus a six-diameter extension at the other end, engaging peripheral longitudinal bars, with the 90-degree hook ends alternated on successive ties, called?
n: A crosstie has a seismic hook at one end and a 90° hook at the other, alternated along the column.

q: The Code requires the minimum thickness of a solid cantilevered slab to be the larger of 100mm and:
n: One-way cantilever slabs need at least L/10.

q: What is the term for a permanent roofed structure attached to and supported by a building, projecting over a public right-of-way?
n: A marquee is a permanent roofed structure over a public way, attached to a building.

q: For non-prestressed concrete beams and columns not exposed to weather or in contact with earth, what is the minimum concrete cover?
n: Beams and columns not exposed to weather or ground need 40 mm of cover.

q: What is the minimum tie or hoop diameter required for bundled bars?
n: Bundled bars and bars 36 mm need ties of at least 12 mm.

q: In cast-in-place work, spirals confining 16mm through 32mm longitudinal bars must have a bar diameter of at least ___.
n: Cast-in-place spirals must be at least 10 mm in diameter.

q: What is the minimum bend diameter specified for reinforcing bars sized 28mm, 32mm, and 36mm?
n: Bars 28–36 mm need an 8db bend diameter.

q: In Figure 1, the reinforcement labeled A refers to the:
n: Label A points to the vertical longitudinal bars of the column: the main rebars.

q: What is the label B pointing to in Figure 1's reinforcement detail?
n: Label B points to a horizontal loop around the column bars: a lateral tie.

q: Based on Figure 1, how deep is the excavation shown?
n: The dimension from grade line to the bottom of the footing is 2 m.

q: Which footing type is depicted in Figure 1?
n: One footing carries two columns, so it is a combined footing.

q: The column type illustrated in Figure 1 is best classified as:
n: The columns have closed ties at intervals, so they are tied columns.

q: Referring to Figure 2, column C-1 has how many main reinforcing bars?
n: C-1 shows 4 bars, one at each corner.

q: In Figure 2, how many main bars does column C-2 have?
n: C-2 shows 6 bars.

q: How many main bars does column C-3 in Figure 2 contain?
n: C-3 shows 8 bars.

q: The columns shown in Figure 2 fall under which classification?
n: Square sections with rectangular ties are tied columns.

q: Under the NSCP, what is the minimum number of longitudinal bars in a column with rectangular or circular ties?
n: Four within rectangular or circular ties, three within triangular ties, six inside spirals. The Code fixes the count, not the bar size.

q: Under the NSCP, what is the minimum number of longitudinal bars in a column enclosed by spirals?
n: Six inside spirals or circular hoops of special moment frames, against four inside ordinary ties.

q: The slab labeled S-1 in Figure 3 is classified as a:
n: S-1 is 1.75 × 4 m: m = 1.75/4 = 0.44, below 0.5, so it is one-way.

q: In Figure 3, slab S-2 is identified as a:
n: S-2 is 2 × 4 m: m = 2/4 = 0.5, so it is two-way.

q: How is slab S-3 in Figure 3 categorized?
n: S-3 is 4 × 4 m: m = 1.0, two-way.

q: Slab S-4 shown in Figure 3 belongs to which category?
What slab type is S-5 in Figure 3?
n: S-5 is 2 × 6 m: m = 0.33, one-way.

q: Figure 3's slab S-6 is best described as a:
n: S-6 is 4 × 6 m: m = 0.67, two-way.

q: For a one-way solid slab with one end continuous, what is the minimum thickness?
n: Simply supported L/20, one end continuous L/24, both ends continuous L/28, cantilever L/10 (for fy = 420 MPa).

q: Older codes set a minimum two-way slab thickness as the panel perimeter divided by what?
n: The old rule was h = perimeter ÷ 180. NSCP 2015 now uses tables based on span and edge beams.

q: What is the minimum thickness of a two-way slab without beams and without drop panels (a flat plate)?
n: Flat plates need 125 mm; with drop panels 100 mm is allowed.

q: For S-1, when neither weather-exposed nor ground-contacted, the required minimum concrete cover is:
n: Slabs not exposed to weather or ground need 20 mm of cover.

q: What are the bars laid at right angles to the main bars of a one-way slab called?
n: Temperature (shrinkage) bars control cracking in the direction the slab does not span.

q: In Figure 3, what bar diameter is specified for the top and bottom bars of slab S-6?
n: The drawing calls for 12 mm bars. The NSCP itself fixes cover, spacing and steel area for slabs, not a minimum bar diameter.

q: Slab design calculations are typically performed on a basis of:
n: Slabs are designed as a 1 m wide strip, so loads and steel are per linear metre.

q: What term describes a slab that rests directly on columns without supporting beams?
n: A flat slab rests directly on columns, usually with drop panels or column capitals.

q: Which stress primarily governs the design of slabs as structural members?
n: Slabs are thin bending members, so flexural stress governs.

q: What is the sudden shaking of the earth from a release of energy at a hypocenter below an epicenter called?
n: Magnitude measures energy released. Intensity (I to XII on the Mercalli scale) measures effects at a place.

q: Ground rupture during an earthquake is most likely to occur along a:
n: Ground rupture happens where the fault reaches the surface.

q: Looking at Figure 4, how far apart are grid points 3A and 3B?
n: Grid A to B is marked 6 m.

q: What is the spacing between grid lines 2B and 2C in Figure 4?
n: Grid B to C is marked 8 m.

q: In Figure 4, what is the total distance from 1A to 1D?
n: 6 + 8 + 6 = 20 m from A to D.

q: How far apart are grid points 2C and 2D per Figure 4?
n: Grid C to D is marked 6 m.

q: What is the diagonal distance between 2A and 3B shown in Figure 4?
steps: 2A to 3B: Δx = 6 m (A to B), Δy = 4 m (2 to 3)
n: The diagonal of a 6 m × 4 m bay is √52 ≈ 7.21 m.

q: Figure 4 indicates beam BC has a clear span of:
formula: Clear span = c-c span − column width
steps: B to C is 8 m center to center
Columns are 500 mm along X, so subtract 250 + 250 mm
n: Clear span is the center-to-center span less the column width.

q: What clear span does beam CD have according to Figure 4?
formula: Clear span = c-c span − column width
steps: C to D is 6 m center to center
n: Clear span is the center-to-center span less the column width.

q: Between grid points 1A and 1B, the beam's clear distance is:
formula: Clear span = c-c span − column width
steps: A to B is 6 m center to center
n: Clear span is the center-to-center span less the column width.

q: The clear span of the beam connecting 1B and 1C measures:
formula: Clear span = c-c span − column width
steps: B to C is 8 m center to center
n: Clear span is the center-to-center span less the column width.

q: What is the clear distance for the beam between 1D and 2D?
formula: Clear span = c-c span − column width
steps: 1 to 2 is 4 m center to center, along Y
n: Along Y the columns are 300 mm, so 4.0 − 0.3 = 3.70 m.

q: In Figure 5, item A (the stirrups/hoops) is otherwise known as:
n: The stirrups (A) are the beam's web reinforcement, resisting shear.

q: Item B in Figure 5's beam detail refers to the:
n: B points to the longitudinal bars: the main bars.

q: For beam cover C in Figure 5, when the beam is neither weather-exposed nor earth-contacted, the minimum is:
n: Beams not exposed to weather or ground need 40 mm of cover.

q: If the beam in Figure 5 is cast directly against earth, cover C must be at least:
n: Concrete cast against earth needs 75 mm of cover.

q: When the main bars in Figure 5 are bundled, what stirrup/hoop diameter is required?
n: Ties or stirrups around bundled bars must be at least 12 mm.

q: Bundling is prohibited for reinforcing bars exceeding what diameter?
n: Bars larger than 36 mm may not be bundled in beams.

q: For the simply supported beam in Figure 5 under a uniform load w (N/m) over span L (m), which formula gives the maximum deflection?
n: For a simply supported beam with uniform load, δmax = 5wL⁴/384EI at midspan.

q: At the supports of the simply supported beam in Figure 5, the deflection equals:
n: Supports of a simple beam do not move vertically, so deflection there is zero.

q: Where along the simply supported beam in Figure 5 does the maximum deflection occur?
n: The deflection of a symmetric simple beam is greatest at midspan.

q: What are the top reinforcing bars of the beam in Figure 5 referred to as?
n: Continuous longitudinal bars at top and bottom are the main bars.

q: Based on Figure 6, which footing(s) shown qualify as combined footings?
n: CF1, CF2 and CF3 each carry more than one column, so all are combined footings.

q: What thickness of gravel base is used beneath the combined footings in Figure 6?
n: The sections note a 100 mm (about 4 in) gravel base.

q: What bar diameter is specified for the footing reinforcement in Figure 6?
n: All bars in the footing details are ø16.

q: Figure 6 shows CF2 with an overall depth of:
n: Section 2E shows CF2 as 400 mm deep.

q: In Figure 6, what is the overall depth of footing CF1?
n: Section 2D shows CF1 as 500 mm deep; CF2 and CF3 are 400 mm.

q: What shape best describes footing CF3 in Figure 6?
n: CF3 is 2,800 × 2,600 mm: a rectangle.

q: CF1's minimum required concrete cover, per Figure 6, is:
n: Footings cast against earth need 75 mm of cover.

q: In Figure 6, what top reinforcement does CF3 have?
n: The CF3 detail calls for 6-ø16 longitudinal and transverse top bars.

q: What column type applies to every column shown in Figure 6?
n: The columns have ties, so they are tied columns.

q: In Figure 7, how many longitudinal bottom bars does CF1 have?
n: Section 1B lists 10-ø16 longitudinal bottom bars at 230 mm; the 15-ø16 are transverse bottom bars.

q: In the transverse direction, how many bottom bars does CF1 have per Figure 7?
n: Section 1B lists 15-ø16 transverse bottom bars at 275 mm.

q: How many topmost bars run in the transverse direction of CF1?
n: Section 1B lists 12-ø16 transverse top bars at 350 mm (and 9-ø16 at 260 mm).

q: In Figure 7, how thick is footing CF1?
n: The bottom dimension of section 1B is 400 mm. The 150 mm is the floor slab and 100 mm the gravel base.

q: What thickness is specified for the Lower Ground Floor Slab in Figure 7?
n: The lower ground floor slab is dimensioned 150 mm.

q: What minimum concrete cover applies to the Footing Tie Beam (FTB) in Figure 7?
n: A footing tie beam cast against earth needs 75 mm of cover.

q: What span length does truss T2 in Figure 8 have?
n: The overall dimension of T2 is 9,800 mm.

q: What material is the truss depicted in Figure 8 fabricated from?
n: Angle sections (L and double-L) mean a steel truss.

q: What is the length of each panel on the left side of the strut line in truss T2?
formula: Panel length = segment length ÷ number of spaces
steps: Left of the strut: 4 equal spaces = 4,350 mm
n: 4,350 mm in 4 equal spaces gives 1,087.5 mm per panel.

q: What cross-section size is used for the web members to the right of the strut in Figure 8?
n: Right of the strut the web members are L75x75x6.0 mm.

q: In Figure 8, what is the U-shaped element at the right end of truss T2 (detail 1E)?
n: The U-shaped channel at the eave catches roof runoff.

q: Among the bars used in the stair design, what is the largest diameter specified?
n: The largest bars called out are ø16.

q: What is the smallest main bar diameter used in the stair design shown?
n: Main bars are ø12 and ø16; the ø10 bars are only nosing bars.

q: Figure 9's stair detail indicates the building has how many storeys?
n: The section shows lower ground, ground and second floors.

q: For design purposes, stairs are treated structurally like a:
n: A stair flight spans like an inclined slab.

q: In Figure 9, what supports the stair landings?
o: Nothing; they cantilever from the wall
n: Each landing sits on an STB1 stair beam at its edge.

q: Which scale rates earthquake intensity from I to XII by observed effects, which weaken with distance from the epicenter?
n: Intensity describes shaking at a place; magnitude (Richter, moment) describes energy at the focus. PHIVOLCS uses its own PEIS, also I to X.

q: What term describes the slow, ongoing strain change under sustained stress, caused by elevated temperature or repeated pounding?
n: Creep is slow strain growth under sustained stress.

q: A framing system is classified as a ___ when its beam-column connections are assumed rigid enough to preserve the original angles between members.
n: A rigid frame keeps the angles between members unchanged under load.

q: What value is used for the modulus of elasticity of structural steel?
n: Structural steel has E = 200 GPa.

q: For pin-connected tension members, the pin diameter must be at least ___ of the eyebar width.
n: Pins in eyebars must be at least 7/8 of the eyebar body width.

q: What joining method fuses built-up member components together in a controlled atmosphere, forming a triangular cross-section?
n: A fillet weld has a roughly triangular cross-section in the corner of two parts.

q: What is the term for the average of a roof's eave height and its highest point elevation (using the eave height itself when the roof slope is 10° or less)?
n: Mean roof height is the average of eave and ridge heights (the eave height if slope ≤ 10°).

q: What Importance Factor value applies to essential facilities?
n: Essential facilities use I = 1.5; special occupancies 1.25; standard 1.0.

q: What classification applies to a structure whose walls are at least 80% open?
n: An open building has each wall at least 80% open.

q: Which wind exposure category applies where flat, unobstructed water extends upwind at least 1,500 m, or 20 times the building height?
n: Exposure D is the roughest wind case: smooth water, mud flats, salt flats or ice running 1,500 m or more upwind, so wind arrives with nothing to slow it.
